brave.title: Trump administration wins 7-2 Supreme Court ruling in political ad dispute
brave.snippet:
The Supreme Court has handed the Trump administration a 7-2 win in an escalating fight over discounted political advertising rates ahead of the midterm elections. In an unsigned order issued Wednesday in FCC v. Brown, the justices blocked a Fourth Circuit ruling that would have required the Federal Communications Commission to resolve a challenge to its political advertising policy within 48 hours.
Four Democratic candidates, Sherrod Brown, Jon Ossoff, Roy Cooper and Kristen McDonald Rivet, have challenged FCC guidance extending those discounted rates beyond candidates themselves to political parties engaged in coordinated spending and some joint fundraising committees. The Supreme Court said the Fourth Circuit went too far when it ordered the agency to make a final decision within two days.
The Supreme Court said the Communications Act appeared to require the full FCC to decide the candidates' administrative challenge before they could seek review in federal court. ... Because Brown, Ossoff, Cooper and McDonald Rivet went to court while their application remained pending at the FCC, the Court said the Fourth Circuit likely lacked statutory jurisdiction to hear their challenge.
"The Fourth Circuit's decision to issue an 'extraordinary' writ was inappropriate under the circumstances," the Court wrote. It added that federal law requires the FCC to rule on applications before it, but "does not obligate the Commission to act within a particular time frame." Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson said they would have denied the stay. ... Newsweek has contacted the FCC and lawyers for the candidates for comment and is awaiting their responses. The U.S. Supreme Court is seen from the front in Washington, D.C.

# FCC v. Brown, 610 U.S. \_\_\_ (2026)
**Docket No.** 26A476

**Decided:** October 14, 2026

**Justia Summary**
Several congressional candidates challenged a public notice issued by the Media Bureau of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) regarding the lowest unit charge (LUC) requirements for campaign advertisements. The notice expanded LUC eligibility to include political candidates, joint fundraising committees with noncandidate members, and political parties engaged in coordinated activity. The candidates argued that only political candidates should be entitled to the LUC, seeking review from the full FCC and, while their application was still pending, filed a petition for review in federal court.
The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit heard the petition for review and found jurisdiction to consider the challenge. The panel granted the petition and set aside the FCC’s public notice, reasoning that the statutory text and legislative history limited LUC eligibility to political candidates. Subsequently, the Fourth Circuit issued a mandamus order requiring the FCC to resolve the candidates’ application within 48 hours, believing this was necessary to facilitate judicial review.
The Supreme Court of the United States reviewed this case following an application by the FCC to stay the Fourth Circuit’s mandamus order. The Court found that the FCC had met the requirements for a stay, including a likelihood of irreparable harm and a fair prospect of success on the merits. It held that the issuance of a writ of mandamus was inappropriate, as the Communications Act does not require the FCC to act within a specific timeframe, and the agency retains discretion over its procedures.
The Supreme Court stayed the Fourth Circuit’s order pending disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari, and clarified that the stay would terminate if certiorari is denied or upon the Court’s judgment if granted.

Supreme Court Justices Seem Skeptical of Nondelegation Doctrine Claim in FCC v. Consumers’ Research

  In 2021, a coalition including a telecommunications carrier subject to the surcharge challenged the program’s constitutionality. The group argued that Congress violated the Legislative Vesting Clause of Article I of the Constitution by granting the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) significant authority both to define the scope of the USF program and to set the quarterly surcharge through which the program is funded, without providing an intelligible principle to guide the agency’s discretion.

  Many court watchers saw this as a potential sleeper case. Although the Supreme Court has only struck down two statutes under the nondelegation doctrine—both in 1935—individual Justices have shown interest in revisiting the doctrine as part of the Court’s recent moves to rein in the administrative state. In  Gundy v. United States  , Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote a dissent (joined by Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Clarence Thomas) that would have created a more robust nondelegation doctrine. Justice Samuel Alito did not join the dissent but supported the effort, and Justice Brett Kavanaugh (who was recused in  Gundy ) later signaled his support as well. In the right case, it seems a majority of the Court could reanimate what many view as a toothless doctrine.

What Fishing Boats and the Supreme Court Have to Do with Undermining the FCC | TechPolicy.Press

  Chevron deference is named for a landmark Supreme Court case from 1984,  Chevron USA Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. It has been a bedrock principle of administrative law from its inception 40 years ago.

  Without  Chevron , courts themselves will need to determine the proper interpretation of a statute. An agency’s interpretation will matter only if the non-expert judges find the agency’s reasoning persuasive when considering potential statutory interpretation. This residual level of deference is called  Skidmore  deference, after a Supreme Court case called  Skidmore v. Swift & Co , decided in 1944 . 

  Industry groups have challenged the FCC’s 2024 order placing broadband internet access service (“BIAS”) back under Title II of the Communications Act, and defining it as a telecommunications service or common-carrier service. The FCC has had deference on this kind of decision before because of a seminal case called  National Cable & Telecommunications Association v. Brand X Internet Services , which held that  Chevron applies when the FCC makes these kinds of regulatory classification decisions. Gorsuch’s concurrence called out  Brand X as an example of “how bad”  Chevron can get. But the deference in  Brand X  to the FCC on such a technical question is essential for regulating internet companies — lest Congress have to introduce new laws every single time a new technology is developed.

  Even without relying on deference to the agency’s interpretation of the Communications Act, a reasonable court should come to the same conclusion as the FCC because BIAS is best classified as a telecommunications service.

# SCOTUS Stays Ruling in FCC Political Ad Rate Suit  
In *Federal Communications Commission v. Brown*, 610 U.S. \_\_\__ (2026), the U.S. Supreme Court stayed a Fourth Circuit order that would have required the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to quickly decide a challenge to its “public notice” extending favorable advertising rates to political parties and joint fundraising committees. The decision means that the FCC does not have to rule on the dispute prior to the November elections.
## **Supreme Court’s Decision**  
The Supreme Court granted the Application for Stay by a vote of 7-2. In its per curiam opinion, the Court held that the Fourth Circuit had improperly exercised its mandamus authority.  
In reaching its decision, the Court emphasized that mandamus is a “drastic and extraordinary” remedy reserved for exceptional circumstances. Such relief generally requires a showing that the petitioner has no adequate alternative remedy and a clear and indisputable right to relief.  
The Court explained that although the Communications Act requires the FCC to resolve applications for review, it does not establish a specific deadline for doing so. The Commission therefore retains discretion over the procedures and timing of its administrative decisions.  
The Fourth Circuit’s order, which required the FCC to issue a final decision within 48 hours while its deliberations were ongoing, exceeded the appropriate limits of judicial intervention.
The Court also concluded that the FCC would suffer irreparable harm if forced to abandon its ongoing deliberative process to comply with the accelerated deadline. That disruption could not be remedied after the fact. Accordingly, the Supreme Court stayed the Fourth Circuit’s October 7 order pending further proceedings.

On September 4, 2026 – the first day of the lowest unit charge (LUC) window for the November general election – the U.S. Supreme Court granted an emergency stay of the Fourth Circuit’s order in *Brown v. FCC,* thereby reinstating the Federal Communications Commission (FCC or Commission) Media Bureau’s March 2026 Public Notice on LUC for political party ads. The Public Notice clarified that authorized committees of legally qualified candidates for federal office and coordinated expenditures between political party committees and legally qualified candidates for federal office are both entitled to LUC.

**Background**

Under LUC requirements, broadcasters must provide candidates with the lowest advertising prices the station charges in the 45 days before a primary election and the 60 days before a general or special election.

This obligation arises under Section 315(b)(1) of the Communications Act, which states:
